court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
holding_summary: HPD must provide relocation assistance to tenants displaced by a vacate order regardless of whether the dwelling units were lawfully configured. The illegality of the rooming/SRO conversion does not defeat tenant status under the Administrative Code and RPAPL definitions.

quotes.text: The vacate order charged that the dwelling had conditions rendering it dangerous to life and unfit for human habitation, including an illegal apartment created in the basement and illegal rooming units and/or single room occupancies on the first and second floors.
RPAPL 711 [“tenant” includes “an occupant of one or more rooms in a rooming house”]

court: Civil Court of the City of New York
holding_summary: A resident who continuously occupies an SRO hotel room as a principal residence for at least six months is a "permanent tenant" entitled to rent-stabilization protection, regardless of who pays the rent, while transient hotel occupants remain outside coverage.

quotes.text: Section 2520.6 (j) of the RSC defines a “permanent tenant” for hotel-housing purposes as an individual who continuously resides in the same building as a principal residence for at least six months.
The existence of an agreement that HRA would pay petitioner rent on respondent’s behalf, if petitioner could prove it, would not preclude respondent from being a permanent rent-stabilized tenant.
the RSC does not apply to hotels or rooms for transient occupants

notes: Turns on the hotel/transient-occupant carve-out from rent stabilization; bears on duration-of-occupancy classification.

holding_summary: An ambiguous Occupancy Agreement for a licensed SRO/community residence, construed against its drafter, required the operator to commence legal eviction proceedings rather than use self-help to remove a resident terminated from the program.

quotes.text: “[n]othing contained herein shall be construed to create a relationship of landlord and tenant between the owner/operator of the [residence] and the resident.”

holding_summary: The court held that a 1982 amendment to the Rent Stabilization Law repealed the statutory authority underlying the owner-use-recovery ground in both the Rent Stabilization Code and the METHISA hotel/rooming-house code, so an owner could not recover a roomer's single-room unit for the owner's own use under either regulatory scheme.

quotes.text: In this holdover proceeding petitioner seeks possession of respondent’s single-room dwelling unit for her own personal use.

the METHISA Code applies not only to these hotel premises but to “similar dwelling units which are subject to regulations pursuant to the ETPA [Emergency Tenant Protection Act of 1974] including units in hotels, single room occupancy facilities and rooming houses, or rooming units”
Whether governed by the Rent Stabilization Code or by the METHISA Code petitioner has no right to recover respondent’s unit for her own use.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term
holding_summary: The Appellate Term held that buildings designed and intended as two-family private dwellings cannot be unilaterally converted into multiple dwellings/rooming houses for single-room occupants, reversing a trial court that had allowed such a conversion and rebuking it for legitimizing illegal, hazardous overcrowded conversions.

quotes.text: this case involves the issue of whether buildings designed and intended to be used as two-family homes (private dwellings) can be unilaterally converted to multiple dwellings for single room occupants.

Administrative Code of the City of New York § D26-33.07 (a) prohibits the creation of a "rooming unit" if it was not so created or classified prior to April 30, 1956 in a "tenement, converted dwelling or private dwelling".
the trial court exalted and legitimized illegal conversions by landlords to overcrowded residences without any consideration for the ensuing danger to life and health.

holding_summary: The court held the owners of a single-room-occupancy rooming house in willful civil and criminal contempt for failing to comply with consent orders requiring repair of numerous Housing Maintenance Code violations affecting the habitability and security of the rooming house.

holding_summary: A former employee who continued to reside and pay rent in his employer's rooming house for six months after his employment ended became a statutory tenant under RPAPL 711, entitled to legal process before eviction; the employer's self-help lockout and removal of his belongings constituted an unlawful eviction supporting an award of damages for emotional distress.

quotes.text: Section 711 of the Real Property Actions and Proceedings Law provides that an occupant of one or more rooms in a rooming house in a city having a population of one million or more, who has been in possession for 30 consecutive days or longer is a tenant.
Section 711 further provides that a tenant shall not be removed from possession except in a special proceeding.
